To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The association of environmental contexts with drugs of abuse leads to persistent drug-cue associations that can be measured using the conditioned activity model of drug-cue learning.

(1) cocaine-cue memories are expressed in the frontal cortex and basolateral amygdala, (2) these cocaine-context memories are maintained via a mechanism that requires NMDA receptor activity and (3) this mechanism involves Arc expression in these same brain regions.

(1) the CA and CPP models both induce a similar profile of Arc expression in the brain; and (2) the NMDA-receptor dependent expression of Arc in the CA model is required for cocaine cue memory persistence.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the neural basis of drug memory and the role of these memories in addiction and relapse.
the molecular mechanisms of drug-cue memory formation and extinction.
understanding how memories of drug-cues contribute to relapse and how these memories can be disrupted.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the present study establishes the involvement of an Arc-dependent NMDA receptor signaling pathway in cocaine-cue memories, and that the conditioned activity (CA), a non-preference based paradigm, is a useful model for the investigation of drug-cue memory.
this study provides evidence that the CA model may be useful in studies of drug-cue memory and suggests the involvement of an Arc-NMDA receptor pathway in memory interference.
(1) both CPP and CA models can be utilized to examine the neural substrates underlying cocaine-cue memory, and (2) the NMDA-receptor dependent Arc pathway is involved in cocaine-cue interference.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Arc expression is a marker of the neural plasticity underlying cocaine-context memory retrieval.
we used a non-preference based model to examine the neural substrates underlying the retrieval of a drug-cue memory.
the CA paradigm is a valid model to study the neural substrates underlying the formation, retrieval and maintenance of drug-cue memory.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the conditioned activity (CA), a non-preference-based, contextual memory model, can be used to investigate the neural mechanisms of cocaine-context memory.
both the CPP and the CA models can be used to study the neural substrates involved in the formation of cocaine-context memories.
both the CPP and non-preference based CA model can be used to study the neural basis of drug-cue memory, and that the NMDA-dependent pathway may be involved in maintaining these memories.
